# Wi-Fi basics

## How 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz differ
<!-- id: wb.en.bands | facts: wb.bands | src: docs/wifi_generations_compare.md; general: Wi-Fi band characteristics | aliases: 2.4ghz vs 5ghz, 6ghz, which band is better, which band to use, difference between bands, what is 5g wifi | say_for: define,compare | say: 2.4 GHz reaches furthest and goes through walls best but is slow and crowded; 5 GHz is much faster but weakens through walls; 6 GHz is very fast near the router but has the shortest range. -->
2.4 GHz reaches furthest and goes through walls best, but it is slow and crowded, shared with many devices and even microwaves and Bluetooth. 5 GHz is much faster with less interference but weakens quickly through walls. 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E and later) is the widest and least crowded, very fast near the router, but has the shortest range and only newer devices use it. Note: "5G Wi-Fi" usually means the 5 GHz band, not the 5G mobile network.

## Which band suits which device
<!-- id: wb.en.choose | facts: wb.choose | src: general: Wi-Fi band characteristics | aliases: which band for my device, which band for a camera, smart home 2.4, tv on 5ghz, device far from router, choose a band, which band should my phone use, which band should I connect to | say_for: judge,howto | say: Devices near the router that need speed are best on 5 GHz or 6 GHz; devices far away behind several walls do better on 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz depending on signal. -->
Devices near the router that need speed (a 4K TV, a game console, a laptop) are best on 5 GHz or 6 GHz. Devices far away behind several walls do better on 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz depending on signal. Cameras, smart plugs and bulbs often support only 2.4 GHz, so keep 2.4 GHz on. When the router and the device both support multi-link (MLO), the device uses several bands at once by itself.

## What MLO (multi-link) is
<!-- id: wb.en.mlo | facts: wb.mlo | src: docs/wifi8_features.md; docs/wifi_generations_compare.md | aliases: mlo, multi-link, multi link operation, several bands at once, wifi 7 mlo | say_for: define | say: MLO (Multi-Link Operation) came with Wi-Fi 7: one device connects to the router over several bands at once, so it is faster, with less delay and fewer drops. -->
MLO (Multi-Link Operation) arrived with Wi-Fi 7: one device connects to the router over several bands at once, for example 5 GHz and 6 GHz. It is faster, with less delay and fewer drops, because when one band is busy or weak the data goes over the other. Both the router and the device must support it.

## How Wi-Fi 6, Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 differ
<!-- id: wb.en.gens | facts: wb.gens | src: docs/wifi_generations_compare.md §2; esp32/main/ui/ui_wifi_compare.c | aliases: wifi 6 vs wifi 7 vs wifi 8, compare wifi generations, difference between wifi 6 and 7, wifi generations, top speed of each standard | say_for: compare | say: Wi-Fi 6 serves many devices at once, Wi-Fi 7 uses several bands at once so it is faster, and Wi-Fi 8 makes real-world speed steadier with fewer drops and less lag. -->
Each generation has one strength: Wi-Fi 6 serves many devices at once without slowing down; Wi-Fi 7 uses several bands at once, so it is faster with less delay; Wi-Fi 8 makes the speed you actually get steadier in every room, with fewer drops and less lag. Wi-Fi 8's theoretical top speed equals Wi-Fi 7's; that is the maximum of the standard, not of one device (iGate A86-C: up to 11.5 Gbps).

## Do older devices work with a Wi-Fi 8 router
<!-- id: wb.en.compat | facts: wb.compat | src: esp32/main/ui/ui_wifi_compare.c | aliases: will my old phone connect, backward compatible, do i need a new phone, wifi 5 device, wifi 6 device on wifi 8 | say_for: judge | say: Yes. Older devices connect to a Wi-Fi 8 router as before; to get every Wi-Fi 8 benefit the device must support Wi-Fi 8 too. -->
Yes. Older phones and laptops (Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6, 7) connect to a Wi-Fi 8 router as before. They get the router-side benefits; to get every Wi-Fi 8 benefit the device must support Wi-Fi 8 too. You do not need a new device to use the network.

## What signal strength is good
<!-- id: wb.en.rssi_levels | facts: wb.rssi_levels | src: esp32/main/ui/ui_wifi_signal.h (signal grades, user 2026-11-10); Router_App/router_context_src/kb/src/metric_glossary.en.md (mg.en.rssi) | aliases: what rssi is good, is my signal strong, is -70 dbm good, signal levels, good rssi, weak signal | say_for: judge | say: An RSSI of −55 dBm or better is good, −56 to −70 fair and enough for video, −71 to −75 weak, and below −75 bad and likely to be slow or drop. | judge: rssi_dbm -55 good, -70 fair, -75 weak, bad -->
RSSI is in dBm, a negative number; closer to 0 is stronger. The router uses four grades, with the same colours as the signal icon on its screen: −55 dBm or better is good (green); −56 to −70 fair, enough for video and calls (yellow); −71 to −75 weak, may be slow or choppy (orange); below −75 bad, likely to drop (red). Real speed also depends on interference, band and device. A reading of 0 dBm from the router means no measurement, not a strong signal.

## Where to put the router
<!-- id: wb.en.placement | facts: wb.placement | src: general: Wi-Fi placement guidance; Router_App/router_context_src/kb/src/troubleshooting.en.md (ts.en.slow.s2) | aliases: where to put the router, router placement, weak signal in far room, better coverage, boost wifi | say_for: howto,judge | say: Put the router in the middle of the home, at chest height or higher, in the open, not in a cabinet, behind the TV or next to metal. -->
Put the router in the middle of the home, at chest height or higher, in the open, not inside a cabinet or behind the TV. Keep it away from metal, large mirrors, aquariums and microwaves. Every wall, concrete ones especially, and every floor weakens the signal clearly; 5 GHz and 6 GHz weaken faster than 2.4 GHz. Multi-storey or long homes do better with an extra access point (mesh).

## Interference and crowded channels
<!-- id: wb.en.interference | facts: wb.interference | src: general: Wi-Fi interference; docs/wifi8_overview.md §3.2 | aliases: wifi interference, neighbours wifi, crowded channel, slow in the evening, many networks around, change channel | say_for: define,howto | say: Neighbours' Wi-Fi, microwaves and Bluetooth can cause interference, especially on 2.4 GHz; move important devices to 5 GHz or 6 GHz. -->
Neighbours' Wi-Fi, microwaves and Bluetooth devices share the airwaves and can make the network slow or choppy, especially on 2.4 GHz and in the evening when every home is online. To reduce it, move important devices to 5 GHz or 6 GHz and keep the router away from sources of interference. The router chooses and changes channels itself when it sees interference, so a device may occasionally drop for a few seconds and reconnect. Wi-Fi 8 adds a way to avoid the busy part of a channel (NPCA).

## Private (random) MAC addresses
<!-- id: wb.en.randommac | facts: wb.randommac | src: docs/device_labels.md §1; general: private Wi-Fi address on phones | aliases: random mac, private address, private wifi address, shows as a new device, lost label, still connects after block, mac changes | say_for: define | say: Newer phones often use a private MAC address that changes per network or over time, so the router may see the phone as a new device. -->
Newer phones often use a "private Wi-Fi address": for each network, or after a while, the phone uses a different MAC address. The router knows devices by MAC, so when it changes the phone appears as a new device and earlier labels, blocks or limits no longer apply. For your home network you can turn off the private address for that network in the phone's Wi-Fi settings. A MAC whose second digit is 2, 6, A or E is usually such a self-assigned address.

## Plan speed, Wi-Fi speed and real speed
<!-- id: wb.en.speeds | facts: wb.speeds | src: Router_App/router_context_src/kb/src/metric_glossary.en.md (mg.en.link); docs/speedtest.md | aliases: plan speed, why not my plan speed, mbps vs mb/s, real speed, wifi slower than plan, phone test lower | say_for: compare | say: There are three different numbers: the plan speed, the Internet line speed to the router and the Wi-Fi speed to your phone; your phone sees the smallest. -->
There are three different numbers: the plan speed (what the provider sells), the Internet line speed to the router (measured by "Check the network quality") and the Wi-Fi speed between the router and your phone (depends on signal, band and device). What your phone sees is the smallest of them. Units: Mbps is megabits per second, MB/s megabytes per second; 100 Mbps downloads only about 12.5 MB/s.

## When to add an access point (mesh)
<!-- id: wb.en.mesh | facts: wb.mesh | src: docs/wifi8_overview.md §3.3; esp32/main/ui/ui_showcase_slides.c (coming soon page) | aliases: mesh, extra access point, range extender, multi-storey home, wifi does not reach, repeater | say_for: judge | say: If a multi-storey or thick-walled home has rooms below about −75 dBm with the router in the middle, add an access point (mesh), ideally linked by cable. -->
If a multi-storey, long or thick-walled home has rooms below about −75 dBm even with the router in the middle, add an access point (mesh) linked to the router, ideally by cable. Cheap range extenders (repeaters) often cut the speed. Seamless roaming between several iGate access points is on the roadmap, not on the current router.
